questions.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere ${x\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are $15,$ $10,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere ${x\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse ${Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ is $15,$ we obtain

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax{‖}^{2}}=15\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax‖}=\sqrt{15}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{15}.$

questions.problem: A $2\times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere ${x\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ ${\sigma }_{2}=4,$ and ${\sigma }_{3}=0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere ${x\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ from ${R}^{3}$ onto the ellipse ${Ax\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ in ${R}^{2}.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $Ax$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where ${x}^{T}({A}^{T}A)x$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix ${A}^{T}A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of ${A}^{T}A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is ${\sigma }_{1}=6,$ the largest eigenvalue of ${A}^{T}A$ must be ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}={6}^{2}.$ So, we obtain that

$$
{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax{‖}^{2}}={6}^{2}\,⟹\,{max}_{‖x‖=1}{‖Ax‖}=6.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is ${\sigma }_{1}=6.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14077831/assets/2d1cefc0c789518d21279c5c49a18f80220a2aad80973f0e84fda0ddaf25493b.png)

A $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle ${x\,|\,‖x‖=1}$ from ${R}^{2}$ onto an ellipse in ${R}^{2}.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A,$ which of the following is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $100$ of ${A}^{T}A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\,…,{v}_{n}}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of ${R}^{n}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}\ge {\lambda }_{2}\ge …\ge {\lambda }_{n}.
$$

Then,

- ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{1},$

- ${\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}$ is the length of $A{v}_{2},$

- $⋯$

In our example, we see that

- $||A{v}_{1}||=10={\sigma }_{1},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{1}={10}^{2}=100,$ and

- $||A{v}_{2}||=8={\sigma }_{2},$ which means that ${\lambda }_{2}={8}^{2}=64.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=100$ of ${A}^{T}A$ is ${v}_{1}.$

canonical_examples.problem: A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Given that the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are $7, 2,$ and $0,$ find the length of the ellipse's semi-major axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$

Since the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ is $7,$ we obtain

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 7
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\}  = \sqrt{7}.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sqrt{7}.$

canonical_examples.problem: A $2 \times 3$ matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Given that the singular values of $A$ are $\sigma_1=4,$ $\sigma_2=2,$ and $\sigma_3 = 0,$ find the length of the semi-major axis of the ellipse.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ maps the unit sphere $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the ellipse $\big\{ A\mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2.$

First, let's re-write the squared distance from the origin to the point $A\mathbf{x}$ on our ellipse, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Ax{‖}^{2} & =(Ax)^{T}(Ax) \\  & =({x}^{T}\,{A}^{T})(Ax) \\  & ={x}^{T}\,({A}^{T}\,A)x,\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $\mathbf{x}^T (A^T A) \mathbf{x}$ is the quadratic form with the symmetric matrix $A^T A.$ 

The maximum value of this quadratic form, when $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A^T A.$ 

The square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^T A$ are called the *singular values* of $A.$ Since the largest singular value of $A$ is $\sigma_1=4,$ the largest eigenvalue of $A^T A$ must be $\lambda_1 = \sigma_1^2=4^2.$ So, we obtain that

$$
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \|^2 \big\} = 4^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\max\limits_{\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1} \big\{ \| A\mathbf{x} \| \big\} = 4.
$$

 

Therefore, the semi-major axis of our ellipse is $\sigma_1=4.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving Problems Regarding the Image of the Unit Eigenvectors of a Quadratic Form
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14077831/assets/094b6043b9cce7f3ac2a7cc32fa53785d3fbf5b490ce853474f89bb4afa8291a.png)

A $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ maps the unit circle $\big\{ \mathbf{x} \,|\, \| \mathbf{x} \| =1 \big\}$ from $\mathbb{R}^2$ onto an ellipse in $\mathbb{R}^2.$ The corresponding ellipse and its principal axes are depicted in the diagram above. Given that $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ are unit eigenvectors of $A^TA,$ find an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $36$ of $A^T A?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is an $m\times n$ matrix. Let 

$$
\left\{\mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2\,\ldots, \mathbf v_n\right\}
$$

be an *orthonormal* basis of $\mathbb R^n$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $A^T A$ with corresponding eigenvalues 

$$
\lambda_1\geq \lambda_2\geq \ldots \geq \lambda_n.
$$

Then,

- $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{\lambda_1}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_1,$

- $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{\lambda_2}$ is the length of $A\mathbf v_2,$

- $\cdots$

In our example, we see that

- $||A\mathbf v_1|| = 8 = \sigma_1,$ which means that $\lambda_1 = 8^2 = 64,$ and

- $||A\mathbf v_2|| = 6 = \sigma_2,$ which means that $\lambda_2 = 6^2 = 36.$

Therefore, an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = 36$ of $A^T A$ is $\mathbf{v}_2.$
